title: Trump directs federal contractors to coordinate with White House on congressional requests for information
content: President Donald Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information on their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration — a move that Democrats say is unlawful as they prepare to launch investigations into his administration next year. An executive order signed by the president Friday said contractors must “abide by any instructions received from the White House and contracting agency related to the withholding of communications that the White House or the agency has determined are protected by executive privilege.” “If the executive branch cannot be assured that those communications will remain confidential, agencies and the White House will be chilled from sharing sensitive information with contractors, which will stymie the operation of critical Government programs,” the executive order argues. The order warns contractors that their agreements with the federal government could be terminated if they fail to comply with its directives. It also accuses certain congressional leaders of “harassing private companies that contract with the federal government” for information and reminds them that their probes must have a “valid legislative purpose.” Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin, who is poised to chair the House Judiciary Committee when Democrats take control in January, called the executive order “unprecedented and blatantly unlawful.” “Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions,” Raskin said in a statement Saturday. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs. After two years of MAGA Republicans in Congress colluding with Trump Inc., accountability and the Rule of Law are coming.” Democrats have mused about investigations into the work Trump has ordered across Washington, DC, including the construction of the White House ballroom, the repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and the planned renovations of the Kennedy Center. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who will chair a key Senate investigative panel, earlier this month sent letters to a slew of companies asking them to cooperate with a planned inquiry into the ballroom. The Connecticut senator previously requested from the construction firm carrying out the project information about the ballroom’s anticipated cost and how it came to chosen as the builder. Democrats have also said they will seek to address the influx of contracts the Department of Homeland Security has granted in Trump’s second term. “Once we have control, then there’s a lot more we can do on guardrails,” Rep. Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, has told CNN, referring to bringing the funds under his committee’s oversight. While still in the minority in Congress, Democrats have sought to investigate the department’s controversial purchasing of planes and contracts to aid Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation operations, as well as contracts for the construction of additional border wall in Big Bend National Park . DHS also came under scrutiny last year after ProPublica reported that a firm run by the husband of the agency’s chief spokesperson, Tricia McLaughlin, was subcontracted to produce an advertising campaign for the department in a $200 million deal. McLaughlin told ProPublica at the time that DHS had no visibility into which subcontractors were selected and that she recused herself because of the conflict of interest. Friday’s directive marks the latest guidance put out by the White House in anticipation of Democrats’ investigations. White House counsel Will Scharf last week penned a memo stating that executive agencies and departments within the Trump administration must obtain approval from the White House before any personnel agree to testify before Congress. More broadly, the White House has taken a combative approach to the planned oversight of the administration. Scharf last week wrote Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, saying that the administration “ will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.” In a separate letter to Democratic committee leaders, Scharf stated that Trump administration officials do not have to comply with demands to preserve or turn over records because of those Democrats’ current status in the congressional minority. Garcia condemned the president’s order on Saturday. “Today’s executive order is the latest in the Trump Administration’s blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional right to conduct oversight,” Garcia said in a post on social media. “What is the White House trying to hide? Donald Trump wants to stop us from exposing the rampant waste, fraud, and corruption by his Administration, but we’re just getting started.” Meanwhile, a top Congressional Democrat on Friday warned that lawmakers will withhold government funding for systems developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX if the Trump administration and tech billionaire refuse to disclose who is responsible for ordering the slowdown of Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink satellite service — the subject of another potential investigation next year. This story was updated with new details. CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez, Audrey Ash, Annie Grayer, Katelyn Polantz, Zachary Cohen and Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

title: Russia-bound ship attacked in Gulf of Finland
content:
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

title: The Democrats’ top 9 targets for investigations next Congress
content: Democrats will soon take over both the House and the Senate. And thanks to President Donald Trump’s lax approach to governmental ethics and disregard for norms, rules and laws, they’ll confront a veritable smorgasbord of investigative opportunities. But that also presents the Democrats with a dilemma: What do they even focus on? The American people seem to have a somewhat limited appetite for investigations , with a Pew Research Center poll this week showing 67% are more worried that congressional Democrats will investigate “too much,” rather than “not enough (31%). And launching a bunch of probes might just mean Americans can’t really focus on any of them. So which ones to focus on? Here are the nine that seem to make the most practical and political sense for Democrats to pursue. The administration has said these strikes target drug traffickers who are “ unlawful combatants .” But even some Republicans have been rubbed the wrong way by what are, for all intents and purposes, extrajudicial killings. That was especially the case after it emerged that the military had conducted a second, “double-tap” strike on an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean. Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia has said he reviewed the available evidence and found that the strikes likely illegally killed “ individuals who are not involved in narcotrafficking .” The downside here for Democrats is that they might not want to look like they’re standing up for alleged drug-traffickers. But these strikes are just so extraordinary that it would seem derelict to not at least try to get more information about them. Trump knocked down the East Wing of the White House with no warning, despite saying that he wouldn’t . His administration kept trying to put his name on the Kennedy Center — and then hid the building’s façade when a judge ordered it removed. And the drama at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool involves an apparently hasty — and certainly botched — job that was done without a competitive bidding process. (Not to mention the indictment of a man who was apparently charged in order to bolster Trump’s baseless claims of vandalism, just to have the Justice Department later drop the case.) And that’s just what we know about. This one is dicey because Elon Musk is the world’s richest man, and it risks looking like retribution over his spending hundreds of millions of dollars to elect Republicans. But there are legitimate investigative targets. So much of Musk’s DOGE efforts were chaotic and hamstrung the functioning of the federal government . And more recently, there have been questions about whether Musk or the Trump administration was responsible for Starlink being throttled and hampering Ukraine’s war defense . Given how much Musk benefits from federal contracts, you could sure make an argument that it’s important to get to the bottom of these things. It’s not just the failed indictments against New York Attorney General Letitia James, January 6 witness Cassidy Hutchinson and six Democratic members of Congress; it’s also the investigations against so many other Trump foes that seemed to be based on so little evidence. The attempt at retribution is completely unmistakable . And as much as anything, Democrats might feel this is an area of needed accountability — for fear of the US political system devolving into an endless series of legal reprisals. This is the most recent scandal, yes. But it also involves extremely high stakes. It implicates the company (Nvidia) that’s perhaps most important to the AI race. It also involves possible Chinese espionage against that company, the possible illegal funneling of coveted AI chips to China (by Megaspeed) and — according to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department shockingly refusing to blacklist Megaspeed , even as his lax approach to such things appeared to benefit a family business . (The Commerce Department has said Lutnick complied with all ethics agreements.) The probe could seek to answer who was told what and when about Megaspeed and Huang’s affair with a Chinese businesswoman, and whether they turned a blind eye to it. This is a very large umbrella. It could involve the killings of immigration protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officials in Minneapolis — which the administration has declined to investigate. It could also involve other potential misconduct , the wrongful arrests and detentions of hundreds of US citizens , the wrongful deportations of still others, and the false claims from the Department of Homeland Security about many of these episodes. Similar to the boat strikes, Democrats might worry about looking too sympathetic to undocumented immigrants, but even Trump has admitted his deportation push wound up being “too tough.” This is also a pretty vast subject, and it feels like much of it has been combed over. But there are plenty of unanswered questions. What did Trump know about Epstein’s actions, and when? (Americans seem to think he knew plenty .) Why did Trump make so many false claims about his proximity to Epstein? Why hasn’t the administration released all of the files? And one of the big ones: How on earth did convicted child sex trafficker Ghislaine Maxwell get a favorable prison transfer after saying helpful things to the DOJ? That last one is almost tailor-made for congressional hearings. And it potentially implicates Attorney General Todd Blanche, who dealt with Maxwell. Perhaps the most obvious target is the administration’s highly inconsistent set of justifications and goals for the war . Similar to the Iraq war, Congress could probe what this was really about — and whether the administration leveled with the American people. We know from reporting by CNN and others that Trump appeared to exaggerate just how imminent a threat from Iran was . Beyond that, Democrats could also probe the US strike on an Iranian elementary school early in the war — which the administration has continued to decline to comment on, claiming its own ongoing investigation. CNN has reported that the available evidence suggests the strike relied on outdated intelligence , and a recent United Nations report found it might have been a war crime . This is both a target-rich environment and one that could pay dividends politically. It’s not just Trump making billions off his presidency through cryptocurrency, promoting stocks he just bought and selling early access to his social media posts . It’s also potential conflicts of interest for Trump’s top overseas negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Lutnick, his commerce secretary . It’s also federal funding that has gone to companies backed by Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm . And most recently, it’s been the possible selling of influence by now-former US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and former top DOJ official Alina Habba. Corruption skyrocketed as a voter concern late in the election, and this is Democrats’ easiest chance to capitalize on that and give voters the accountability they seem to crave on the subject. With the potential for investigations looming, Trump on Friday signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to coordinate with the White House on a response to any congressional inquiries related to their work.
